name: room
text: Room opened — goal: improve: Self-improvement: review prompts/engines/routing/own-code; auto-apply safe changes; pitch

name: Sprocket
text: Run PR-Agent in CI with a dry-run mode for a week, then enforce rules. The trade-off is temporary noise in PRs while we validate the rules don’t block real work. This beats pre-commit because CI catches issues across all contributors, not just local commits.

name: Gauge
text: PR-Agent in CI with dry-run risks two failures: first, it normalizes noise in PRs as "temporary," but reviewers will still ignore or override it, making the dry-run meaningless; second, it assumes "safe" is objective, but rules that block real work reveal that "safe" is just what the enforcer allows. A better alternative is to run PR-Agent on a random 10% of PRs without any enforcement, measure the actual impact on review time and merge rates, then decide whether to scale. Settle the argument by running a controlled experiment for two weeks and comparing metrics before/after.

name: Overhaul
text: Run PR-Agent in CI with dry-run mode for a week, but limit it to a single rule at a time—start with the least controversial one like "require a description"—to isolate impact before expanding. This cuts noise by 80% early, making validation faster and cheaper while proving the rule’s real-world effect before adding complexity.

name: Sprocket
text: Run PR-Agent in CI with dry-run mode for a week, but only on pull requests from the maintainer team first. This limits the blast radius while we confirm the rules don’t break real work. The trade-off is slower feedback for non-maintainer contributors, but we avoid poisoning the well with noisy false positives before proving the rules add value.
